test_title: RRB Group D Previous Year Paper (Held on: 29 Aug 2022 Shift 2)
subject: general
question:
Consider the below statements and identify the correct answer.

**Statement I: **According to Newland's assumption, only 56 elements existed in the nature.

**Statement II:** Newland found that every eighth element had properties similar to that of the first.

options.text: Statement I is correct, Statement II is incorrect.
Statement II is correct, Statement I is incorrect.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Both statements are correct.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points:__**

__
 
• The **atomic masses **of the **elements **were used by Newlands to arrange them.
 
• He noticed that every **eighth **element has the same **attribute **when he grouped the elements in order of their atomic masses.
 
• After every 8 elements, the **same attributes reappear**, giving the law its name, the **Newlands law of octave.**
 
• Then, known elements including **hydrogen, lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, sodium, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, phosphorus, sulphur, **and** chlorine **were placed in order of increasing atomic mass.
 
• This indicates that **lithium and sodium**, the eighth element relative to lithium, have features in common and so on.
 
• He believed that there were only **56 elements** in nature and that **no new elements **will ever be found. 
 
• Later he was proved **wrong**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information:__**

 
• British chemist John Alexander Reina Newlands, who researched on the **periodicity **of **elements**, was born on November 26, 1837, and died on July 29, 1898.
 
• The** first periodic table **of chemical elements **organised **according to their respective **atomic masses **was created by Newlands and published in Chemical News in **February 1863.**
 
• In **1865**, Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner **released **his** "Law of Octaves,"** which declared that "every given element will display analogous behaviour to the eighth element following it in the table," as a continuation of his work with triads and Jean-Baptiste Dumas' families of related components.
